Replica Tensor Train

Miha Srdinšek1⋆\star, Gabriel Gouraud1†\dagger and Xavier Waintal1‡\ddagger

1 Université Grenoble Alpes, CEA, Grenoble INP, IRIG, Pheliqs, F-38000 Grenoble, France

⋆\star mihasrdinsek@gmail.com , †\dagger gab.gouraud@gmail.com , ‡\ddagger xavier.waintal@cea.fr

Abstract

We describe a numerical many-body technique that is based on both tensor networks and quantum Monte Carlo. The variational ansatz is a tensor network that can harvest volume-law entanglement. It is constructed from a tensor train to which one applies a set of non-local operators that force several indices of the tensor train to represent the same physical index, hence its name – replica tensor train (RTT). From the tensor network toolbox, it inherits the possibility to make linear combinations of these states and apply a certain class of operators. We can therefore find the ground-state of a local Hamiltonian in a purely algebraic way as in standard tensor network algorithms – i.e. without using gradient descent methods. On the other hand, the volume-law structure forbids calculating physical observables directly. In much the same way as on a quantum computer where one can prepare a state but can only sample it at the end, here we have to use Markov Chain Monte Carlo to compute the observables. We further show that the approach can be extended to build Krylov-subspace ground-state methods within the variational manifold. We illustrate the different algorithms on a two-dimensional spin model with a transverse magnetic field, which can be solved by this approach at low computational cost.

1 Introduction

Finding the ground-state of a quantum many-body problem is hindered by the exponential growth of the Hilbert space size with the number NN of particles (e.g., spins, qubits, or fermionic sites). It is very tempting, and often effective, to focus on a small part of the Hilbert space, the one we expect to be relevant, i.e. to use a variational approach to the problem. However, not all variational approaches are born equal. The computability, i.e. the mathematical tools at our disposal to compute with them has strong variations with the underlying class of wave functions. A second thing that varies is the expressivity of the ansatz, i.e. its ability to approximate the true ground-state for a given size of the variational manifold. Often, one must compromise and give up some computability in exchange for an increased expressivity.

In terms of computability, the gold standard are arguably the matrix product states (MPS). This one-dimensional tensor network ansatz has everything that one could dream of: it can be sampled exactly, two states can be added together, calculating local observables is straightforward, and we have powerful algebraic approaches to find the ground-state – i.e., the celebrated DMRG algorithm [57, 56]. The only drawback of MPS is that its expressivity is excellent for one-dimensional problems [14, 7], but somewhat limited for two-dimensional problems and beyond. Its two-dimensional tensor network generalization, PEPS, essentially solves the expressivity problem. However, there is a large cost in computability: finding the ground-state becomes a much more complex affair and the computational cost increases drastically [38].

At the other extreme of the spectrum, one finds ansätze with limited internal structure: we only know how to evaluate the unnormalized wave function for a given configuration and, thanks to automatic differentiation, we can easily calculate the gradient of the wave function with respect to its parameters. With such properties, we are left with a unique path for calculating the observables and finding the ground-state: Markov chain Monte Carlo and energy minimization with noisy gradient descent. This approach is known as variational Monte Carlo (VMC) [44, 43, 2]. Since there are almost no constraints for constructing a VMC ansatz, highly expressive ones can be built. A natural choice for such constructions is to use a neural network. For instance, convolutional image processing models that retain a notion of space and locality, and language processing transformer models, which describe complex long-range correlations via an attention mechanism. The resulting neural quantum states (NQS) have become very popular [1, 32, 50, 6, 16, 27, 35, 42, 20, 33, 15, 51, 4, 23]. Despite the field being rather recent, very promising results have been obtained. Yet, we think that it is fair to state that the noisy gradient descent in a non-convex manifold is not ideal: it requires a large number of optimization steps and there is no guarantee of convergence (presence of local minima or barren plateaus).

Researchers on both sides are seeking solutions to this computability-expressivity duality problem. On the NQS side, they try to add more structure. For instance, one can build objects that automatically capture the antisymmetry of the wave function [35] or certain symmetries such as translational invariance [37]. On the tensor network side, one can decrease the computational burden by using Markov Chain Monte Carlo on PEPS [53, 26, 25, 29] or increase the expressivity through String Bond States (SBS) [40, 41, 12] or embed MPS inside NQS [22, 54, 59, 46, 24, 9]. This is a very active and quickly evolving field. Indeed, with the techniques already available to us, there is increasing evidence that we are not far from solving the founding models of the field, such as the Hubbard model [34, 60, 36].

The purpose of this article is to address the above problem through a new mathematical object – we shall call it a Replica Tensor Train (RTT) – that has interesting mathematical properties. As we shall see, the RTT is an extension of MPS that allows one to quite dramatically increase the expressivity of the MPS while keeping some of its core algebraic properties. The main appeal of RTT, and chief result of this paper, is that while it can harvest volume-law entanglement with low bond dimension, we shall be able to find the ground-state within the RTT manifold without resorting to gradient descent.

In a nutshell, an RTT is a long tensor train where several sites of the tensor network correspond to the same physical spin, see Fig.1 for a schematic. The RTT ansatz is introduced in four different, but equivalent ways in section 2:

  • •

    as an MPS where physical indices appear more than once,

  • •

    as an “MPS of MPS”,

  • •

    as a tensor network,

  • •

    and as an MPS embedded in a quantum error correction code (An MPS with a set of stabilizers).

We show that these different formulations provide different insights, allowing us to construct our formalism.

In Section 3, we provide the algorithms for finding the ground-state of a given Hamiltonian. The algorithms are rather peculiar: on the one hand, the ground-state can be constructed in a fully algebraic way using only tensor network tools such as tensor contraction and singular value decomposition (as in the DMRG algorithm). On the other hand, to compute any observable, one must sample the state using Markov chain Monte Carlo. In some sense, the situation is very similar to that of a quantum computer where we can construct the state algebraically using quantum gates, but the sampling of qubits is still needed for measuring anything.

In Section 4, we illustrate the above on a 20×2020\times 20 two-dimensional transverse-field Ising model.

2 Replica Tensor Trains

In this section, we build the Replica Tensor Train (RTT). The RTT is a variational ansatz that has special algebraic properties, which will allow us to build new algorithmic procedures for finding ground-states of many-body systems.

2.1 Preliminary remark: Tensor Trains versus Matrix Product States

The concepts of Matrix Product States and Tensor Trains are used interchangeably in the literature, the former originating from quantum many-body physics and the latter from mathematics. For the purpose of this article, it will be important to properly separate the two concepts. We define a TT (Tensor Train) �i1,…​i\phi_{i_{1},...i} with \Omega discrete variables i1,i2​…​ii_{1},i_{2}...i, where i�∈{0,1}i_{\alpha}\in\{0,1\}, (the generalization to dimensions larger than 22 is trivial) as,

�i1,…​i=𝐓𝐫​A1i1​A2i2​…​Ai.\phi_{i_{1},...i}=\mathbf{Tr}A_{1}^{i_{1}}A_{2}^{i_{2}}\dots A^{i}. (1)

A�i�A_{\alpha}^{i_{\alpha}} is a set of two ��×��+1\chi_{\alpha}\times\chi_{\alpha+1} matrices A�0A_{\alpha}^{0} and A�1A_{\alpha}^{1} (or in tensor network language a tensor with three indices) where, by convention, the first and last bond dimensions ��\chi_{\alpha} are set to unity: �1=� +1=1\chi_{1}=\chi_{\Omega+1}=1. A TT is just a tensor network. It can represent any large tensor �i1,…​i\phi_{i_{1},...i} without, a priori, any connection to a quantum many-body state.

What we call an MPS, on the other hand, is a TT used to represent a quantum many-body state (this was its actual original meaning before these objects started to be used for many new purposes). We consider a system with NN spins, qubits or fermionic occupation states. A basis set for our Hilbert space is |𝒔⟩=|s1​…​sN⟩\ket{\boldsymbol{s}}=\ket{s_{1}...s_{N}} where s�∈{0,1}s_{\alpha}\in\{0,1\} is the state of the chosen spin/qubit. A general quantum state | ⟩\ket{\Psi} takes the form,

| ⟩=∑𝒔s1​…​sN|𝒔⟩.\ket{\Psi}=\sum_{\boldsymbol{s}}{}_{s_{1}...s_{N}}\ket{\boldsymbol{s}}. (2)

We define the MPS as a state where s1​…​sN{}_{s_{1}...s_{N}} is a TT with =N\Omega=N.

In the rest of this section we will construct other quantum states (the RTT), also defined with TTs, but with ≥N\Omega\geq N. In exchange for a much higher expressivity (volume law entanglement), these RTT will loose many, but not all, of the nice properties of MPS. In particular, it will not be possible to compute expectations of observables or of the Hamiltonian exactly using contractions; also it will not be possible to rotate the computational basis trivially. However, some crucial properties will remain such as the possiblity to apply an operator or to add two RTT together.

2.2 Four equivalent definitions of RTT

We now construct the Replica TT quantum state. There are four different but equivalent ways of defining the RTT, each providing different insights which will later be useful in the discussion of different algorithms. These definitions are made in terms of a tensor train where physical sites appear more than once (the pedestrian definition, useful to actually evaluate the ansatz), a matrix product state of matrix product state (useful to make contact with previous ansatz), a tensor network (useful to define algeric operations) and a quantum error corrected matrix product state (a curiosity at this stage that could become useful in the future).

2.2.2 RTT as a nested MPS of MPS

Another way of viewing an RTT is as an "MPS of MPS". For the sake of clarity, let us suppose that the function �​(!)\sigma(\omega) goes through all the physical sites once, then again through all the sites a second time (in a different order), then again until =K​N\Omega=KN. We call such a state an RTT with KK orderings (with KK replicas per site). Defining

�𝒔(i)=A1+i​Ns�​(1+i​N)​A2+i​Ns�​(2+i​N)​…​AN+i​Ns�​(N+i​N)\phi_{\boldsymbol{s}}^{(i)}=A_{1+iN}^{s_{\sigma(1+iN)}}A_{2+iN}^{s_{\sigma(2+iN)}}\dots A_{N+iN}^{s_{\sigma(N+iN)}} (11)

we arrive at,

=𝒔∑�0​…​�K−2[�𝒔(0)]�0[�𝒔(1)]�0​�1⋯[�𝒔(K−1)]�K−2{}_{\boldsymbol{s}}=\sum_{\alpha_{0}...\alpha_{K-2}}\big[\phi_{\boldsymbol{s}}^{(0)}\big]_{\alpha_{0}}\big[\phi_{\boldsymbol{s}}^{(1)}\big]_{\alpha_{0}\alpha_{1}}\cdots\big[\phi_{\boldsymbol{s}}^{(K-1)}\big]_{\alpha_{K-2}} (12)

justifying the name “an MPS of MPS”, as each tensor network [�𝒔(i)]�​�[\phi_{\boldsymbol{s}}^{(i)}]_{\alpha\beta} corresponds to a regular MPS. It follows automatically from this remark that RTT generalizes MPS, as well as String Bond States which are a rank 1 product of MPS. However, this construction shows that an RTT does not only allow for a product of different MPS, but also for any linear combinations between them. Last, since it has been shown that String Bond States naturally encompass Restricted Boltzmann Machine [12], it follows that RTT contains this class of neural networks as well.

2.2.4 RTT as an MPS with quantum error correction

The fourth way of viewing an RTT is to define it as the projection of an MPS on the logical space of a quantum error correction code [30]. Indeed, if we define the stabilizers

Vj​a=ZRj,a​ZRj,a+1V_{ja}=Z_{R_{j,a}}Z_{R_{j,a+1}} (31)

then satisfying the constraint 𝒞\mathcal{C} amounts to enforcing

⟨ |Vj​a| ⟩=+1\bra{\Psi}V_{ja}\ket{\Psi}=+1 (32)

for all the stabilizers. In other words, we can write the projector 𝒞T​𝒞\mathcal{C}^{T}\mathcal{C} as,

𝒞T​𝒞=∏j=1N∏a=1|Rj|−11+Vj​a2.\mathcal{C}^{T}\mathcal{C}=\prod_{j=1}^{N}\prod_{a=1}^{|R_{j}|-1}\frac{1+V_{ja}}{2}. (33)

In the rest of this article, we will not explore the implications of this stabilizer formulation further. However, it could be an interesting avenue for adapting the algorithms of this article to actual quantum hardware. Indeed, there exist efficient quantum circuits for constructing any MPS as well as quantum circuits (using ancilla qubits) for measuring the stabilizers.

2.3 Discussion of the expressivity and volume-law entanglement.

The expressivity of an MPS is directly linked to the value of its bond dimensions since for a given site aa, the quantum entanglement entropy between the two subsystems defined by i<ai<a and i≥ai\geq a is bounded by S≤log⁡�aS\leq\log\chi_{a}. The way we order the tensors may also play an important role [28]. More generally, for an arbitrary TT, the bond dimension controls the amount of "correlations" that can be built between two TT sites; any correlation function must decay exponentially with distance with a correlation "length" �\xi controlled by �\chi. In an RTT, the presence of the replicas bring non-local correlations into the picture: they provide "shortcuts" so that two sites that are close in the physical space have (some) replicas that are also close in the replica space. We therefore have two routes to increase the expressivity of the RTT ansatz: increase the bond dimension and/or add new replicas.

We argue that the RTT ansatz can harvest volume-law entanglement. This point is intuitively very clear: by using enough (∼N/�\sim N/\xi) replicas, any physical site can be arbitrarily correlated with any other physical site. The statement can also be understood algorithmically: if one tries to compress an RTT back into an MPS form using standard tools (writing e.g. the constraints as rank 2 matrix product operators), one expects an exponential increase of the bond dimension. A more formal proof of the assertion follows from previous results of the literature. Indeed, seeing the RTT as a nested MPS of MPS [see Eq. (11)] it follows that "string bond states" are a particular case of RTT. Since these string bond states are themselves a generalization of the Restricted Boltzmann Machine (RBM) [12] and the RBM can exhibit volume-law entanglement [8], it follows that RTT possesses this characteristic too. In that point of view, the replicas play the role of the hidden units in an RBM.

In this article, we restrict ourselves to very specific paths [shown in Eqs. (54, 55)], however, many other paths can be considered depending on the entanglement structure of the targeted quantum state. In the following, we explore how the RTT representation of volume-law states can be learned using different algebraic methods, avoiding the gradient descent typically used in volume-law ansätze such as RBMs and NQS.

3 Finding the ground-state with an RTT ansatz

In this section, we discuss our approach to find the ground-state 0 of a Hamiltonian ℋ\mathcal{H} using an RTT variational ansatz. As we shall see, the technique is very peculiar: the ground-state can be constructed in a purely algebraic way without resorting to gradient descent (in contrast to what is done in VMC). In that sense, the technique to find the ground-state is relatively close to DMRG. On the other hand, in order to compute observables, we need to resort to sampling, i.e. the method becomes stochastic. In that sense, the technique shares similarities with what is usually done in VMC.

Perhaps a good analogy is with quantum computers where the construction of the state is purely deterministic through the application of a sequence of quantum gates. But in order to measure anything, one needs to measure the qubits and the output becomes stochastic.

We will design two distinct routes for obtaining the ground-state. In the first, we work purely in the replica space while in the second we work in the physical space. What we mean by this statement is that in the first technique, we work directly on the object �\phi using the replica space Hamiltonian ℋ¯\bar{\mathcal{H}}. In contrast, in the second technique, we work on \psi using the actual physical Hamiltonian ℋ\mathcal{H}.

3.1 Optimization in the replica space

Our first approach is to use a variant of the power method to find the ground-state of ℋ\mathcal{H}. Starting from an initial RTT (0)=𝒞�(0){}^{(0)}=\mathcal{C}\phi^{(0)}, we define

=(P)(1−�ℋ)P(0){}^{(P)}=(1-\tau\mathcal{H})^{P}{}^{(0)} (34)

By construction (provided �\tau is sufficiently small and the overlap of (0) with 0 is nonzero), (P) converges to the ground-state 0,

0=limP→∞(P){}_{0}=\lim_{P\rightarrow\infty}{}^{(P)} (35)

We seek to represent 0 as an RTT, by using,

(P)=𝒞�(P){}^{(P)}=\mathcal{C}\phi^{(P)} (36)

with,

�(P)≡(1−�​ℋ¯)P​�(0)\phi^{(P)}\equiv(1-\tau\bar{\mathcal{H}})^{P}\phi^{(0)} (37)

So far, the process is exact. However, in its naive implementation, the internal rank �\chi of �(P)\phi^{(P)} may increase very quickly with PP. The actual algorithm alternates the application of 1−�​ℋ¯1-\tau\bar{\mathcal{H}} with compression steps. Indeed, the underlying assumption of the overall approach is that 0 can be approached very precisely with a small value of �\chi.

More precisely, �(P)\phi^{(P)} is created from �(P−1)\phi^{(P-1)} using the following sequence,

  • •

    compute the different contributions �i​ℋ¯i​�(P−1)\eta_{i}\bar{\mathcal{H}}_{i}\phi^{(P-1)} for ∀i∈{1​…​Nℋ¯}\forall i\in\{1...N_{\bar{\mathcal{H}}}\}. The Pauli strings are MPOs with rank 1 so these MPO.MPS multiplications are straightforward and do not increase the rank.

  • •

    sum the different terms together two by two.

  • •

    compress the resulting sums to a targeted rank �\chi (see the algorithm in e.g. Section 5.3.1 of Ref. [52]).

  • •

    repeat the two preceding steps until all the terms are exhausted and one is left with a single TT. Multiply the result by �\tau and subtract it from �(P−1)\phi^{(P-1)} to obtain �(P)\phi^{(P)}.

In other words, the algorithm amounts to performing a form of Time-evolving block decimation (TEBD) with the replica space Hamiltonian ℋ¯\bar{\mathcal{H}}. Other approaches are also possible. For instance, one could try and run the DMRG algorithm on ℋ¯\bar{\mathcal{H}} using an auto-MPO computation followed by a regular DMRG computation leveraging the fact that if �\phi is an eigenstate of ℋ¯\bar{\mathcal{H}} then =𝒞​�\psi=\mathcal{C}\phi is an eigenstate of ℋ\mathcal{H}. In our preliminary exploration, we have found that our TEBD-like approach is effective and although it might be improved, the crucial point does not lie there but in the choice of ℋ¯\bar{\mathcal{H}}. Indeed, as we have mentioned above, there are many different choices of ℋ¯\bar{\mathcal{H}} that correspond to a single ℋ\mathcal{H}. While all are valid choices, the different TT �\phi are not all amenable to the same level of compression. We will experiment with different possible choices in the next section.

3.2 Optimization in the physical space

As we shall see, the preceding technique has some limitations in terms of precision in its current form. The reason is that the algorithm works blindly: one does not compute the energy of the state until the very end, so the effect of the compression on the energy is unknown and cannot be mitigated.

While the algorithm in the preceding subsection was close in spirit to the power method, we now introduce an algorithm that resembles the Lanczos Krylov technique. Let \psi be our current approximation of the ground-state 0 and let 𝒪�\mathcal{O}_{\alpha} be a set of operators. For instance, to recover a variant of the Lanczos algorithm, we use 𝒪�=ℋ�−1\mathcal{O}_{\alpha}=\mathcal{H}^{\alpha-1} but we will consider also other operators. By convention 𝒪1=1\mathcal{O}_{1}=\mdmathbb{1} is the identity operator. The algorithm goes as follows. First, we construct the products �=𝒪� {}^{\alpha}=\mathcal{O}_{\alpha}\psi, by using 𝒪¯�\bar{\mathcal{O}}_{\alpha}, as done in the replica space optimization. Second, we seek the new approximation of the ground-state ′ in the form of an optimal linear combination of these states,

′=∑�c��.{}^{\prime}=\sum_{\alpha}c_{\alpha}{}^{\alpha}. (38)

Because RTTs are by construction not normalized, we also need to introduce the constraint that the state has to be normalized. ′ is then the solution of the generalized eigenvalue problem

H​c=�​S​c,Hc=\lambda Sc, (39)

with the lowest eigenvalue. The Hamiltonian matrix H�​�H_{\alpha\beta} and the overlap matrix S�​�S_{\alpha\beta} are expressed in the reduced basis

H�​�\displaystyle H_{\alpha\beta} =\displaystyle= �†ℋ�\displaystyle{}^{\alpha\dagger}\mathcal{H}{}^{\beta} (40)
S�​�\displaystyle S_{\alpha\beta} =\displaystyle= �†�,\displaystyle{}^{\alpha\dagger}{}^{\beta}, (41)

with the normalization enforced by c†​S​c=1c^{\dagger}Sc=1, where c=(c1​c2​…)c=(c_{1}c_{2}...) represents the vector of the coefficients c�c_{\alpha}. This small eigenvalue problem (we typically consider fewer than ten operators 𝒪�\mathcal{O}_{\alpha}) is readily solved and it yields the new approximation ′ of the ground-state. If we wish to continue with another optimization step, we turn ′ back to an RTT form by summing the TTs ��\phi_{\alpha}. The final �′\phi^{\prime} can also be compressed.

The important difference between this scheme and the one of the preceding section is that we need to compute the matrix elements H�​�H_{\alpha\beta} and S�​�S_{\alpha\beta}. These computations will involve a stochastic approach. Indeed, while in principle these matrix elements could be computed through a direct contraction of the associated tensor network, it is unfeasible in practice as the cost is exponential in NN. In the next section, we show how a simple adaptation of the variational Monte Carlo algorithm, which we call dual Monte Carlo (because it involves sampling both |�|2|{}_{\alpha}|^{2} and |�|2|{}_{\beta}|^{2}), solves this problem.

3.3 Dual Monte Carlo

The remaining problem is the following: given two RTTs 1 and 2, how can we compute the matrix elements 1†ℋ2{}^{1\dagger}\mathcal{H}{}^{2} and 1†2{}^{1\dagger}{}^{2}. The following algorithm is actually very general and does not require the states to be RTTs, it would work equally well for e.g. neural quantum states. Although not widely spread, similar algorithms have already been developed in the literature [31, 48].

Using Markov Chain Monte Carlo (e.g. the Metropolis algorithm), we can sample the probability distribution P𝒔P_{\boldsymbol{s}} defined as,

where readers familiar with VMC will recognize inside the average ⟨⋯⟩P𝒔1\langle\cdots\rangle_{P_{\boldsymbol{s}}^{1}} over the distribution P1P^{1} a quantity similar to the local energy used in VMC. where MM is the number of states �. In practice, we have found that it is often sufficient to re-orthogonalize with respect to the first vector 1 only. As an example of a dual Monte Carlo calculation, a matrix S�​�S_{\alpha\beta} before (left) and after (right) re-orthogonalization is shown in Fig.2.

This concludes the general description of the algorithm. We note that although dual Monte Carlo is very handy, it is not strictly speaking necessary: since the optimization performed on the c�c_{\alpha} is done on a handful of parameters, one could use a standard variational Monte Carlo for this very small problem (a typical number we have used so far is M≤5M\leq 5). The key aspect of the physical optimization is our ability to select a handful of important MM directions for finding the ground-state (typically guided by the Hamiltonian), as opposed to using a gradient on thousands or hundreds of thousands of parameters.

4 Application to the 2D transverse Ising model

We now turn to an actual calculation to illustrate the above RTT approach on a practical example. We consider the transverse field Ising model with nearest-neighbor interactions on a square lattice of N=L×LN=L\times L spins. The Hamiltonian is defined as,

ℋ=∑⟨i,j⟩Zi​Zj−hx​∑iXi,\mathcal{H}=\sum_{\langle i,j\rangle}Z_{i}Z_{j}-h_{x}\sum_{i}X_{i}, (53)

where ⟨i,j⟩\langle i,j\rangle represents the sum over all the nearest-neighbor pairs of sites. We use open boundary conditions. The interest in this model stems from different aspects. First, as a function of the transverse magnetic field hxh_{x} the model undergoes a quantum phase transition, from the paramagnetic to the antiferromagnetic phase which breaks the Z2\mdmathbb{Z}_{2} symmetry [55, 49]. This is a paradigmatic example of a quantum phase transition. The transition is furthermore accompanied by a classical phase transition at finite temperature. Second, these types of models have recently received a lot of interest in the context of quantum annealing [39, 10, 5]. The quantum annealers based on Rydberg atoms, in particular, are described by Eq. (53) with slightly longer range interactions. Third, we have already established in a previous publication that String Bond States with very low rank are extremely efficient ansätze for this model [46]. Since RTT generalizes String Bond States, it follows that RTT must as well be very efficient for this problem. Our goal below is merely to illustrate the new algebraic approach described in the preceding section, we postpone the study of more difficult models to future publications.

4.1 Specification of the algorithm

To specify the algorithm entirely, we need to specify two things: the path (i.e. the function �​(!)\sigma(\omega)) and the operators 𝒪�\mathcal{O}_{\alpha}.

4.1.1 Specification of the path

We use a path that first goes through all the sites column by column (VV for Vertical), then line by line (HH for Horizontal), then diagonally (DD) then along the other diagonal (D′D^{\prime}).

More formally, we introduce the different paths �V\sigma^{V}, �H\sigma^{H}, �D\sigma^{D} and �D′\sigma^{D^{\prime}} defined graphically as,

.\vbox{\hbox{\includegraphics[width=207.0021pt]{figures/orderings.pdf}}}. (54)

The global path �​(!)\sigma(\omega) of our RTT is

�=�H​V​D​D′≡�V⊕�H⊕�D⊕�D′\sigma=\sigma^{HVDD^{\prime}}\equiv\sigma^{V}\oplus\sigma^{H}\oplus\sigma^{D}\oplus\sigma^{D^{\prime}} (55)

It follows that for a given site ii, Ri​1R_{i1} is the TT index of this site in the horizontal ordering, Ri​2R_{i2} corresponds to VV, Ri​3R_{i3} to DD and Ri​4R_{i4} to D′D^{\prime}. The open paths that we used are well adapted to the open boundary conditions of the model. These paths would require adaptation to be used for a model with periodic boundary conditions in order to keep the prescription that "sites close by physically should have replicas that are close by somewhere in the replica space".

4.1.2 Definition of the operators in the physical space

Second, we need to define the operators 𝒪�\mathcal{O}_{\alpha}. We use only local operators that include at most two Pauli matrices. Our convention is the following: we write �=(A,B)\alpha=(A,B) where AA indicates which Pauli matrix is concerned (for instance A=Z​ZA=ZZ for product of two ZZ operators and A=XA=X for a single XX operator). For pairs of Pauli strings, BB labels the direction of the bond (VV, HH, DD, D′D^{\prime}, possibly combinations such as V​HVH if both vertical and horizontal bonds are considered). For instance, nearest neighbour Z​ZZZ operators along the vertical direction are noted,

𝒪Z​Z,V=∑i=(ix,iy)Z(ix,iy)​Z(ix,iy+1)\mathcal{O}_{ZZ,V}=\sum_{i=(i_{x},i_{y})}Z_{(i_{x},i_{y})}Z_{(i_{x},i_{y}+1)} (56)

while along the diagonal direction, they are noted,

𝒪Z​Z,D=∑i=(ix,iy)Z(ix,iy)​Z(ix+1,iy+1).\mathcal{O}_{ZZ,D}=\sum_{i=(i_{x},i_{y})}Z_{(i_{x},i_{y})}Z_{(i_{x}+1,i_{y}+1)}. (57)

Likewise the transverse field operator reads,

𝒪X=∑i=(ix,iy)X(ix,iy)\mathcal{O}_{X}=\sum_{i=(i_{x},i_{y})}X_{(i_{x},i_{y})} (58)

With these notations, the transverse field Ising Hamiltonian reads,

ℋ=𝒪Z​Z,V+𝒪Z​Z,H−hx​𝒪X.\mathcal{H}=\mathcal{O}_{ZZ,V}+\mathcal{O}_{ZZ,H}-h_{x}\mathcal{O}_{X}. (59)

4.1.3 Definition of the operators in the replica space

Next, when we commute the ZiZ_{i} operators with the Kronecker circuit 𝒞\mathcal{C}, we have several choices for the definition of 𝒪¯�\bar{\mathcal{O}}_{\alpha} i.e. we can decide where we move the ZiZ_{i} operators. We use the notation →C\rightarrow C where C=V,H,D,D′C=V,H,D,D^{\prime} to indicate on which part of the RTT the ZiZ_{i} are sent. This is not the most general choice, here we assume that all the ZiZ_{i} operators of a given operator are sent to the same part of the RTT. For instance, for the example of the 𝒪Z​Z,V\mathcal{O}_{ZZ,V} operator, we might decide to send the ZiZ_{i} to the vertical part of the path (this is the natural path that works best in practice),

𝒪¯Z​Z,V→V=∑i=(ix,iy)ZRi,2​ZRi=(ix,iy+1),2\bar{\mathcal{O}}_{ZZ,V\rightarrow V}=\sum_{i=(i_{x},i_{y})}Z_{R_{i,2}}Z_{R_{i=(i_{x},i_{y}+1),2}} (60)

but we could also decide to send them to the diagonal part of the path,

𝒪¯Z​Z,V→D=∑i=(ix,iy)ZRi,3​ZRi=(ix,iy+1),3\bar{\mathcal{O}}_{ZZ,V\rightarrow D}=\sum_{i=(i_{x},i_{y})}Z_{R_{i,3}}Z_{R_{i=(i_{x},i_{y}+1),3}} (61)

There is no such freedom for the 𝒪X\mathcal{O}_{X} operator, so we simply have,

𝒪¯X=∑i=(ix,iy)XRi,1​XRi,2​XRi,3​XRi,4.\bar{\mathcal{O}}_{X}=\sum_{i=(i_{x},i_{y})}X_{R_{i,1}}X_{R_{i,2}}X_{R_{i,3}}X_{R_{i,4}}. (62)

Note that in these numerical experiments we limit ourselves to using operators in the replica space that are obtained using the commutation rules derived earlier. This is important for replica space optimization to guarantee that the replica Hamiltonian has the same eigenstates as the physical one. However, no such constraint exists for physical space optimization where we may use any operator we want. This freedom may be used for e.g. optimizing a particular tensor A(i)A^{(i)} (or a pair of tensors) without resorting to gradient descent. Another remark is that if all the operators contain only ZiZ_{i} Pauli matrices, then Dual Monte Carlo is not needed – a single Monte Carlo simulation provides all the needed matrix elements (since all the different states share the same probabilities).

4.2 Replica space optimization

We now present the result of some numerical experiments where we apply the operator 1−�​ℋ¯1-\tau\bar{\mathcal{H}} iteratively PP times on an initially constant TT �(0)\phi^{(0)} (�𝐢(0)=1∀𝐢\phi^{(0)}_{\mathbf{i}}=1\ \ \forall\mathbf{i}). Importantly, the algorithm to obtain �(P)\phi^{(P)} is perfectly deterministic. However, to obtain the physical observable (here the energy), we need to resort to VMC stochastic sampling. In all the remaining, the corresponding statistical errors are always negligible compared to the error due to the ansatz being imperfect. Only the latter is discussed. The results are shown in Fig. 3 for hx=3h_{x}=3, a point very close to the quantum critical point [55, 49], hence supposedly the most difficult to compute. The reference ground-state energy E/N=−3.18185±0.00004E/N=-3.18185\pm 0.00004 for this point was obtained using the Green Function Monte Carlo algorithm and a perceptrain ansatz as discussed in [46]. We choose the smallest non-trivial rank for the RTT, �=2\chi=2. One should keep in mind that tensor network calculations are typically performed with much higher ranks in the hundreds or thousands. We use three different choices of ℋ¯\bar{\mathcal{H}}. The first is

ℋ¯H=𝒪¯Z​Z,H→H+𝒪¯Z​Z,V→H−hx​𝒪¯X\bar{\mathcal{H}}_{H}=\bar{\mathcal{O}}_{ZZ,H\to H}+\bar{\mathcal{O}}_{ZZ,V\to H}-h_{x}\bar{\mathcal{O}}_{X}\\ (63)

This choice corresponds to sending all the operators to a single sub-MPS part of the RTT. Therefore, it does not exploit the full freedom of the RTT but rather works as a regular MPS. We find that the error barely decreases to an error �​E/E≈6×10−2\delta E/E\approx 6\times 10^{-2} consistent with what one obtains with a regular MPS for such a small rank. The situation improves drastically when one sends the different interaction terms to the parts of the RTT where they are local, i.e. when we use,

ℋ¯H​V=𝒪¯Z​Z,H→H+𝒪¯Z​Z,V→V−hx​𝒪¯X.\bar{\mathcal{H}}_{HV}=\bar{\mathcal{O}}_{ZZ,H\to H}+\bar{\mathcal{O}}_{ZZ,V\to V}-h_{x}\bar{\mathcal{O}}_{X}. (64)

We find that the error drops by more than one order of magnitude reaching �​E/E≈3×10−3\delta E/E\approx 3\times 10^{-3}, an error level where the physics of the ansatz is qualitatively correct. It is still possible to improve on these results in a variational manner in order to take advantage of the diagonal parts of the RTT DD and D′D^{\prime}. For instance, if we add one more operator with a parameter �\alpha,

ℋ¯H​V​D​D′=ℋ¯H​V+�​(𝒪¯Z​Z,D→D+𝒪¯Z​Z,D′→D′),\bar{\mathcal{H}}_{HVDD^{\prime}}=\bar{\mathcal{H}}_{HV}+\alpha\left(\bar{\mathcal{O}}_{ZZ,D\to D}+\bar{\mathcal{O}}_{ZZ,D^{\prime}\to D^{\prime}}\right), (65)

we find that the error reaches �​E/E≈10−3\delta E/E\approx 10^{-3} for the optimum choice of the parameter �=0.08\alpha=0.08. In the various experiments that we have performed, we have found that the curves shown in Fig. 3 are very generic: the descent is fast, robust and independent of the initial state or choice of metaparameters. The error levels that we have achieved are consistent with those found using VMC and gradient descent using the technique described in [46] for, respectively, K=1K=1 (MPS level), K=2K=2 (two subparts of the RTT are active) and K=4K=4 (the diagonal parts are also active). The advantage of the present approach is that we bypass entirely the non-convex optimization problem. We have also checked that the method works robustly across different system sizes in Fig. 4 where we observe that the error barely increases while going from a 6×66\times 6 system to a 20×2020\times 20 one. This is in sharp contrast to plain MPS where the error deteriorates dramatically at fixed rank (see section 4.5). For the ℋ¯H​V​D​D′\bar{\mathcal{H}}_{HVDD^{\prime}} replica space Hamiltonian, the value �=0.08\alpha=0.08 was found to be close to optimum across the three system sizes. The optimum value of �\alpha was found by a simple 1D scan of �\alpha, these calculations being rather light computationally.

4.3 Physical space optimization

We now turn to physical space optimization using the dual Monte Carlo technique. We start from the RTT \psi obtained using replica space optimization with the ℋ¯H​V\bar{\mathcal{H}}_{HV} replica space Hamiltonian Eq.(64) and seek the best linear combination Eq.(38) using certain operators. Based on the results of the replica space optimization, we expect the important operators to be those that involve the diagonal part of the RTT but we will work in an agnostic way to see how the method works in practice. We will use 44 operators: identity, 𝒪¯X\bar{\mathcal{O}}_{X}, 𝒪¯Z​Z,H​V=𝒪¯Z​Z,H→H+𝒪¯Z​Z,V→V\bar{\mathcal{O}}_{ZZ,HV}=\bar{\mathcal{O}}_{ZZ,H\to H}+\bar{\mathcal{O}}_{ZZ,V\to V} and 𝒪¯Z​Z,D​D′=𝒪¯Z​Z,D→D+𝒪¯Z​Z,D′→D′\bar{\mathcal{O}}_{ZZ,DD^{\prime}}=\bar{\mathcal{O}}_{ZZ,D\to D}+\bar{\mathcal{O}}_{ZZ,D^{\prime}\to D^{\prime}}. The results are shown in Table 1 for various choices of the operators included in the calculation. We find an improvement (of the same order as in the replica space optimization when we considered the ℋ¯H​V​D​D′\bar{\mathcal{H}}_{HVDD^{\prime}} replica space Hamiltonian) whenever the diagonal operator 𝒪¯Z​Z,D​D′\bar{\mathcal{O}}_{ZZ,DD^{\prime}} was included. The main difference with replica space optimization is that in the physical space optimization, we can only improve the energy since we are building, by construction, the best linear combination of the different orbitals. We checked explicitly that the accuracy was not affected by the final compression used to put the linear combination back into an RTT form. Table 1 also includes the rescaled variance of energy, a quantity known as the V-score [58]. These results confirm what was surmized above: the information on the horizontal/vertical paths and transverse field was already included in the replica state optimisation so only the diagonal operator brings an improvement.

The above approach could be extended in various ways by considering more operators. For instance using powers of ℋ¯\bar{\mathcal{H}}, we can build a Lanczos-like method. We could also add operators that favor a given phase (say a staggering operator for the antiferromagnetic phase). We leave the associated explorations to further studies.

Fig. 5 shows different steps of the physical space optimization process. We observe that the convergence happens within a handful of iterations. Also, the eigenvalues of the generalized eigenproblem almost coincide with the result of the Dual Monte Carlo calculation which indicates that the compression performed after solving the linear system does not significantly alter the state.

Fig. 6 shows the error obtained using the same optimization as in Table 1 for a span of the hxh_{x} values in the paramagnetic region of the phase diagram. We find that the error is consistently below �​E/E≈10−3\delta E/E\approx 10^{-3}. We did not study the antiferromagnetic side of the phase diagram which, we surmise, would require the introduction of operators that explicitly break translational symmetry since we expect a boundary phase transition before the bulk one [19]. An interesting feature of Fig. 6 is a relatively large gain in precision obtained in the presence of the diagonal operator 𝒪¯Z​Z,D​D′\bar{\mathcal{O}}_{ZZ,DD^{\prime}} around hx=4h_{x}=4. We attribute this feature to the increase of the antiferromagnetic correlation length as one decreases hxh_{x}: at some point it becomes large enough for the presence of the diagonal correlations to play a significant role. Lowering hxh_{x} further, one would need to add more orderings and/or increase the bond dimension to keep up with the increasingly long-range correlations that build in the system.

4.4 A study of RTT expressivity

The most striking aspect of the previous results is that a very precise energy �​E/E≈10−3\delta E/E\approx 10^{-3} could be obtained with a very low rank �=2\chi=2. A natural question is whether this error can be further decreased and by which mechanism (rank increase or longer paths). In this section we generalize our RTT ansatz, increasing the two parameters that control its expressivity, \Omega and �\chi. There are two sides to the question of reaching higher accuracy: the expressivity of the RTT ansatz itself (with more complex paths and higher rank �\chi) and the optimization process (choice of operators, virtual versus physical optimization etc). Here we study only the first aspect and use plain VMC with gradient descent on the RTT cores for the optimization. Studying the second aspect would require a study of the importance of different operators which we leave for subsequent publications on more challenging models.

Let us start by extending the scope of the studied paths. For our 2D model, a physical site is a point (x,y)(x,y) in the 2D grid so that we write �​(!)=(x⁡(!),y⁡(!)CLOSE\sigma(\omega)=(x(\omega),y(\omega). For most values of !\omega, the horizontal path correspond to �H​(!+1)=�H​(!)+(1,0)\sigma^{H}(\omega+1)=\sigma^{H}(\omega)+(1,0) (we ommit the transition from one line to the next on the boundaries for clarity, see Eq.54). Similarly, the vertical path corresponds to �V​(!+1)=�V​(!)+(0,1)\sigma^{V}(\omega+1)=\sigma^{V}(\omega)+(0,1); the diagonal ones to �D​(!+1)=�D​(!)+(1,1)\sigma^{D}(\omega+1)=\sigma^{D}(\omega)+(1,1) etc.

We label these paths according to the Manhattan displacement distance dd on the lattice. �1\sigma^{1} contains all distance 11 displacements, i.e. (0,1)(0,1) and (1,0)(1,0). With our previous notations �1=�H⊕�V=�H​V\sigma^{1}=\sigma^{H}\oplus\sigma^{V}=\sigma^{HV}. Path �1\sigma^{1} also potentially permit for correlations that connect a physical site to some of its d=2d=2 next nearest neigbours, i.e. (0,±2)(0,\pm 2) and (±2,0)(\pm 2,0) if the TT has a high enough rank. However, it cannot easily describe correlations with sites in the diagonal with displacement (±1,±1)(\pm 1,\pm 1) as these correlations correspond o virtual sites that are ∼N\sim N away. �2\sigma^{2} contains all distance 22 displacements that are not in �1\sigma^{1}, i.e. �2​(!+1)=�2​(!)+(±1,±1)\sigma^{2}(\omega+1)=\sigma^{2}(\omega)+(\pm 1,\pm 1). With our previous notations �2=�D⊕�D′\sigma^{2}=\sigma^{D}\oplus\sigma^{D^{\prime}} so �1⊕�2\sigma^{1}\oplus\sigma^{2} is the most complex path of the previous section. We continue with �3\sigma^{3} that contains all the distance 33 displacements that connot be obtained by following path �1\sigma^{1} or �2\sigma^{2}: �3​(!+1)=�3​(!)+(±1,±2)\sigma^{3}(\omega+1)=\sigma^{3}(\omega)+(\pm 1,\pm 2) and (±2,±1)(\pm 2,\pm 1). The full path up to distance 33 is �1⊕�2⊕�3\sigma^{1}\oplus\sigma^{2}\oplus\sigma^{3}. We also include �4\sigma^{4} and �5\sigma^{5} with similar definitions.

The intuition for this construction is illustrated in Fig. 7 which shows which sites can be reached from the central one using the different paths. The red site is the closest one that cannot be reached directly from the center. As we go from left (�1\sigma^{1}) to right (�1⊕�2⊕�3\sigma^{1}\oplus\sigma^{2}\oplus\sigma^{3}) we observe that this red site moves away from the central one so that all local correlations can easily be described. We therefore anticipate that improving the accuracy requires increasing both dd and �\chi: increasing dd moves the unreachable (red) sites away while increasing �\chi is needed for the information to travel on longer distances in the path.

To check the above intuition, we have optimized various RTT from d=1d=1 to d=5d=5 for the critical point hx=3h_{x}=3. We have used the following procedure: For each distance dd, we construct a �=2\chi=2 RTT(dd) by extending the optimized �=2\chi=2 RTT(d−1d-1) with a rank one constant function for the new part of the path. Then, we optimize the obtained RTT (using standard stochastic gradient descent). Once we reach a plateau, we increase the rank and continue the optimization. Interestingly, the largest fraction of the optimization steps is spent optimizing �1\sigma^{1}, the subsequent optimizations only require around 10% as many steps as the first one.

The results are shown in Fig. 8, where we report the relative energy error �​E/E\delta E/E versus �\chi for different values of dd. We make several observations. First and most importantly, increasing dd and/or �\chi provides a systematic way to decrease the error, from 2. 10−32.\ 10^{-3} down to 5. 10−55.\ 10^{-5}, by almost two orders of magnitude. Second, increasing �\chi is ineffective for �1\sigma^{1} unless �\chi becomes "so high" that even a simple MPS reaches the same accuracy (more on the significance of "so high" in the next section, it is expected to scale exponentially with system size). In contrast, increasing dd by one unit provides a large drop in the error. These two observations are consistent with our hypothesis that the error is dominated by the difficulty to correlate physical sites that are situated in diagonal (the red site in the left of Fig. 7). Third, we observe that the d=2d=2 curve has a much stronger slope than d=1d=1. Again, this is consistent with the fact that the next correlation that need to be captured are the next nearest neighbour along the vertical and horizontal directions, that are already reachable within �1\sigma^{1} provided �\chi is big enough to convey the information. Overall these findings are qualitatively consistent with the intuition behind the schematic of Fig. 7.

4.5 Algorithm complexity and discussion of other methods

As stated earlier, the 2D transverse field Ising model is one of the simplest genuine many-body problem; it can be solved with a variety of techniques including neural quantum states (RBM [1], Transformer [45]), Projector Monte Carlo [18], Green function Monte Carlo [46], stochastic series expansion [21], Path Integral Monte Carlo [17], Tree tensor networks [47] and even plain DMRG for systems not too large [11]. In a recent publication, the authors have solved a similar model for a system as large as 100,000,000 spins using a taylored ansatz and variational Monte Carlo [13]. Our goal at this stage is therefore not to claim any superiority of the RTT (this, we hope, will come in subsequent publications) but more modestly to establish the technique as a new path to ground state exploration.

The number of free parameters in the ansatz is equal to ∼ ​�2\sim\Omega\chi^{2} which is also the computational complexity of evaluating the RTT on a given configuration. From a given configuration, 𝐬\mathbf{s}, there are ∼N\sim N configurations 𝐬′\mathbf{s^{\prime}} for which the Hamiltonian H𝐬𝐬′H_{\mathbf{ss^{\prime}}} matrix element is non-zero. Using NwN_{w} Monte Carlo samples requiring O⁡(N)O(N) Monte Carlo steps for thermalization, the overall cost of the stochastic part of the algorithm is ∼Nw​N​ ​�2∼Nw​K​N2​�2\sim N_{w}N\Omega\chi^{2}\sim N_{w}KN^{2}\chi^{2} for a single matrix elements and ∼Nw​N​ ​�2​M2\sim N_{w}N\Omega\chi^{2}M^{2} for the full eigenvalue problem. For the parameters used in this study, with a Nw=104N_{w}=10^{4}, that translates into 101110^{11} (embarrasingly parallel) operations per steps, a few seconds on a modern multicores CPU. The algebraic part of the algorithms consists of adding ∼N\sim N RTT together, a process whose complexity scales as ​�3\Omega\chi^{3}. Overall replica optimisation scales as ​N​�3\Omega N\chi^{3} per steps, i.e. faster than the Monte Carlo part for �≪Nw\chi\ll N_{w}. However, it typically requires many more step which compensates for the difference in complexity. In our numerical experiments on a computer with 64 cores, for the L=20L=20, hx=3h_{\text{x}}=3 data point, the Replica optimization converges in 15−2015-20 mn of CPU time while the subsequent Physical optimization only takes 1.51.5 mn. For comparaison, obtaining the same accuracy with stochastic gradient descent took roughly 33 hours.

With regards to VMC schemes based on (stochastic) gradient descent, the putative advantage of RTT is twofold. First, typical gradient descent traces require a very large number of Monte Carlo steps. This is highly dependent on the problem, ansatz and optimization methods but tens of thousand steps are typical in machine learning. This is to be contrasted with the rapid convergence of replica optimisation and the handful of steps required by the physical optimisation. Second, so far NQS struggle to learn the sign of the wavefunction in models where a sign problem is present (our ultimate target). A common strategy is to use a smart NQS architecture that already captures this sign to a degree (e.g. using backflow corrections or similar ideas) but recent work indicates that this may come with a bias [3]. Here the hope, that remains to be demonstrated, is that the new techniques associated with the RTT, together with its own peculiar expressivity, will allow one to make progress in learning the sign of the wavefunction.

With regards to DMRG, it is expected that the rank needed to address a 2D system with a simple MPS scales as �∼exp⁡(L)\chi\sim\exp(L) due to the area law. For a 20×2020\times 20 lattice, it is still feasible to brute force the calculation. Ref. [11] actually did it using TPUs (i.e. large computational resources) and very large rank up to �=65,536\chi=65,536 exactly for our reference point hx=3h_{x}=3. They report a variational energy E/N=−3.18197​(2)E/N=-3.18197(2) consistent with ours within our stated error levels. We have repeated these DMRG calculations for smaller bond dimensions. The important point is that, with RTT, we report an accuracy �​E/E∼10−3\delta E/E\sim 10^{-3} that is essentially independent of LL at fixed �=2\chi=2. In contrast, in order to reach the same accuracy �​E/E∼10−3\delta E/E\sim 10^{-3} with MPS, one requires �=32\chi=32 (L=10L=10) and �=256\chi=256 (L=20L=20) i.e. a factor 6464 increase in the number of parameters of the ansatz. RTT reaches the same accuracy with respectively 1.5%1.5\% (L=10L=10) and 0.02%0.02\% (L=20L=20) of the parameter count. These data validate the claim that RTT carries volume law entanglement.

With regards to PEPS and in particular to the recent trend to use Monte Carlo and gradient descent to reduce the computational burden associated with them [53, 26, 25, 29] (one only needs to contract the wave function, not its square, to sample), the RTT ansatz is much lighter computationally. Its evaluation is barely (K×K\times) more complicated than that of a MPS. At this stage, however, we cannot compare the expressivity of the two models nor their trainability.

5 Conclusions

In this work we have introduced a variational ansatz, the Replica Tensor Train, that naturally extends a class of previously discussed powerful ansätze [40, 41, 12, 46]. Our chief result is that RTT has an internal structure that provides the possibility to build the ground-state of a Hamiltonian directly without resorting to gradient descent. We have shown a proof of principle that the method works for the 2D Ising model with transverse field, obtaining a very good accuracy while using a minimal bond dimension �=2\chi=2.

This article opens more new questions than it answers and much more work is needed. The most urgent question is whether the set of new techniques will be efficient to solve more difficult models, notably models with sign problems. Indeed, while VMC is immune to the sign problem, we do not yet have a general approach to learn the sign. The hope is that our global operator based approach will not suffer from the same limitations as local gradient descent. One could also envision combining the two approaches. While we focused on ground-state search, the dynamics, within the time-dependent variational principle framework should also be directly in scope of the operator approach (in either replica and/or physical space). On the technical ground, one needs to study how the quality of the ansatz can be controlled using e.g. higher ranks, more complex paths, more operators and possibly meta algorithms that choose the best combination dynamically. Last, variants of the RTT-based techniques compatible with quantum hardware could also be constructed.
